extractedItems.title: What to do when two balls are very close together
extractedItems.question: Two golf balls are so close together on the fairway that they might block each other's shots. What should you do?

choices.text: Pick up and clean both balls, then play.
Mark and pick up one ball (but don't clean it), play the other ball, then replace the first ball.
Leave both balls where they are and try to play around them.
Remove both balls and drop them at a different location.

extractedItems.explanation: If two balls are so close they obstruct each other, one can be marked, picked up (not cleaned), and replaced after the first is played.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage girl golfer on the fairway, marking her golf ball with a coin because it is very close to another ball.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Girl golfer marks her ball with a coin next to another ball on the fairway.

extractedItems.title: Taking relief for an embedded ball
extractedItems.question: If your ball is embedded in the ground after it lands, what should you do?

choices.text: Leave the ball in place and play it as it lies.
Pick it up, clean it, and drop it within one club-length, no nearer the hole, with no penalty.
Take a two-stroke penalty and drop it anywhere on the green.
Replace it exactly where it embedded.

extractedItems.explanation: You may lift, clean, and drop your ball within one club-length, not nearer the hole, with no penalty if it's embedded.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage boy golfer using a tee to measure a drop spot after his ball is embedded in soft ground.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Boy golfer preparing to drop his ball near an embedded spot on the fairway.

extractedItems.title: Moving loose impediments around your ball
extractedItems.question: Which of these can you do without penalty if loose impediments (like leaves or stones) are near your ball?

choices.text: You can remove them, but if your ball moves, you must replace it and add a penalty stroke.
You can remove them, and if your ball moves, just play from where it ends up.
You cannot move loose impediments near your ball at all.
You can only remove loose impediments with special permission from a referee.

extractedItems.explanation: You may remove loose impediments, but if your ball moves, you must replace it and take a one-stroke penalty.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage boy gently picks up a twig and a small stone from beside his ball on the fairway.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Boy picks up a twig beside golf ball near rough.

extractedItems.title: Dealing with movable obstructions on the course
extractedItems.question: While playing, your golf ball comes to rest against a can. What are you allowed to do?

choices.text: Only play the ball as it lies.
Remove the can and, if the ball moves, put it back without penalty.
Remove the can, and if the ball moves, take a one-stroke penalty.
You must not move the can because it is part of the course.

extractedItems.explanation: Movable obstructions like cans can be removed, and if the ball moves, you put it back without penalty.
extractedItems.imagePrompt: A teenage girl bends down to remove a soda can from beside her golf ball in the rough.
extractedItems.imageAlt: Girl golfer removes a soda can beside her ball on the rough.

reviewedItems.title: What to do when two balls are very close together
reviewedItems.question: Two golf balls are so close together on the fairway that one player's stroke would be affected. What should happen next?

choices.text: Pick up and clean both balls, then play.
Mark and lift the other player's ball (without cleaning it), play your own shot, then replace their ball.
Try to play without moving either ball, even if it's difficult.
Both balls must be dropped in a different spot.

reviewedItems.explanation: When two balls interfere with each other, one player's ball can be marked and lifted (without cleaning). After the other player's shot, the ball is replaced in its original spot.

Remove the can and take a one-stroke penalty if the ball moves.
